boundaries: Most efficacy data comes from retrospective cohorts or small prospective trials; causality is not always established. Biomarker consistency varies across cancer types and populations.
contribution: Summarizes clinical evidence linking specific bacterial taxa (e.g., A. muciniphila, Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium) to improved ICB response rates and survival outcomes in melanoma, NSCLC, and HCC. Details the negative impact of antibiotics and PPIs on ICB efficacy. Provides data on FMT success in reversing resistance.
possible_uses: To support arguments about which microbial signatures predict favorable ICB outcomes and which medications should be avoided. To illustrate the clinical feasibility of microbiome-targeted interventions.

boundaries: Many mechanistic details are derived from mouse models; translation to human physiology may differ. Some mechanisms (e.g., specific metabolite concentrations in TME) are inferred rather than directly measured in all contexts.
contribution: Details specific mechanistic pathways: 1) Direct interaction: Bacteria activating DCs via STING/cGAS pathways and MHC class I upregulation. 2) Metabolite mediation: SCFAs regulating Treg differentiation and HDAC activity; Inosine acting on A2AR; IPA inducing epigenetic reprogramming of CD8+ T cells. 3) Antigen mimicry: Cross-reactivity between bacterial antigens (e.g., TMP1) and tumor antigens (e.g., PSMB4). 4) Systemic inflammation: Role of MAMPs/PAMPs in priming immune responses.
possible_uses: To explain the biological plausibility of microbiome-ICB interactions. To identify specific molecular targets (e.g., STING, A2AR, AhR) for future therapeutic development. To differentiate between direct bacterial effects and indirect metabolite effects.

boundaries: The relationship between specific microbes and irAEs is complex and sometimes contradictory across studies. Treating irAEs (e.g., with steroids) may further alter the microbiome, confounding observations.
contribution: Discusses the dual role of GM in toxicity, identifying taxa associated with increased irAEs (e.g., Ruminococcaceae UCG 13, Turicibacter) and those associated with reduced toxicity (e.g., Bacteroides fragilis, Lactobacillus salivarius). Highlights the link between GM dysbiosis and ICB-induced colitis.
possible_uses: To address the safety profile of ICB and the potential for microbiome modulation to mitigate side effects without compromising efficacy. To explore the correlation between efficacy and toxicity markers.
